disease_info: Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) is a trauma- and stressor-related disorder that develops following exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence, either directly, as a witness, via learning of such events affecting close others, or through repeated exposure to aversive details. It is characterized by intrusive re-experiencing of the trauma, avoidance of reminders, negative alterations in cognition and mood, and marked changes in arousal and reactivity persisting for more than one month and causing significant distress or impairment. PTSD can have an acute, delayed, or chronic course, and is distinguished from acute stress disorder by its duration and from other anxiety or mood disorders by the presence of a clear qualifying trauma and trauma-specific re-experiencing phenomena. Comorbid depression, substance use, and high-risk behaviors are common and can complicate both presentation and treatment.

narrative.personality: She is a meticulous, sustainability-focused architect with a reflective, artistic temperament who usually manages stress through yoga, painting, and time outdoors.
narrative.stressor: Four months ago, Sarah was overseeing a renovation of a historic downtown building when a structural failure caused a partial collapse while she and her team were conducting a site walkthrough. One of the contractors she had worked closely with was severely injured in front of her, and she was trapped for a short time under debris, convinced she might die before being pulled out by emergency responders. In the weeks that followed, she tried to return to work quickly, pushing herself to meet deadlines and insisting on visiting similar sites to prove to herself and colleagues that she was still capable, but her usual coping routines like yoga and watercolor painting felt increasingly hollow and she began taking impulsive risks on job sites and in her personal life. When her firm’s partners confronted her after she drove alone to an unsafe, partially condemned structure late at night to “double-check” details and her ex-husband expressed alarm about her increasingly dangerous behavior, she agreed to seek psychiatric help, realizing that the way she was pushing herself was putting her safety and career at risk.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’ve started doing really risky things without thinking, like going into unsafe buildings alone, and it scares me because I don’t seem to care what happens to me in the moment.”

narrative.personality: He is an easygoing, people-oriented retail worker with a creative streak who loves art, food, and community gatherings, but often carries a quiet undercurrent of worry.
narrative.stressor: About five months ago, Jose was driving his wife and younger cousin home from a late community festival when a speeding truck ran a red light and slammed into the passenger side of their car. He remained conscious and was trapped in the driver’s seat, unable to move, watching his cousin pinned and gravely injured while his wife screamed, and he was certain they would all die before emergency services arrived. Although his cousin survived after a long ICU stay, the accident left Jose feeling responsible, and he tried to cope by throwing himself back into work and community events, telling everyone he was “fine” while avoiding talking about the crash. Over the next four months, however, his normally laid-back manner gave way to frequent, sudden outbursts at customers, coworkers, and even during soccer games at minor frustrations, straining relationships at home and work; after nearly shoving a coworker during an argument over a store display and seeing his wife in tears over how “on edge” he’d become, he agreed to see a psychiatrist.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I keep snapping and yelling at people over nothing since the car accident, and it’s scaring my wife and causing problems at work.”

narrative.personality: He is a steady, routine-loving retiree who values practicality, community involvement, and quiet pastimes, though he tends to worry and resist major changes.
narrative.stressor: Four and a half months ago, Jim underwent what was supposed to be a routine abdominal surgery that was complicated by unexpected bleeding and a brief period of intraoperative instability, leading to an ICU stay where he woke up intubated, disoriented, and intermittently aware of alarms, staff shouting, and his wife crying at his bedside. He later learned that for a time the medical team was unsure if he would survive, and he retained vivid fragments of feeling suffocated, helpless, and unable to communicate while believing he was dying. Once discharged, he tried to return to his orderly routines—gardening, church volunteering, and walks by the river—but nights became increasingly difficult, and he started dreading bedtime, staying up late watching classic movies or pacing the house to avoid the quiet. When his wife noticed how exhausted and irritable he had become, and he admitted he was no longer able to get more than a couple of hours of rest despite his usual habits, they decided to consult a psychiatrist at the suggestion of their primary care physician.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Ever since that surgery in the hospital, I just can’t sleep through the night anymore, no matter how tired I am.”
